title: ephemeral-prefetch-sawtooth-fallback-runbook-draft
body:
Summary:

On 2029-06-12 UTC we observed a repeatable sawtooth pattern in streaming p95/p99 latency for the hosted API. Traffic looked nominal but streaming sessions experienced periodic 2–8s latency spikes lasting ~30–90s, recurring every ~10–12 minutes on affected edge clusters. Impact: customer-facing streaming responses degraded (delayed chunk delivery) for ~6% of traffic from 03:14–07:02 UTC; no broad 5xx wave, but severe QoE degradation for long-running chats.

Why this doc exists:
- Capture the on-call timeline and immediate mitigations we used during the incident.
- Record the emergent root cause hypothesis (ephemeral prefetch/backpressure interaction with edge multiplexing + KV-cache eviction waves).
- Draft a runbook to detect and mitigate the pattern proactively and to provide operators playbook steps for fast recovery.

High-level impact:
- Clients observed delayed tokens (streaming chunk TTFB) and occasional short partial reconnects.
- Latency SLO (p95 streaming chunk TTFB) breached for ~3.5 hours; affected customers reported slow UX but no mass request failures.
- Estimated user-visible sessions impacted: ~6% of streaming sessions in eu-west-1 and us-east-1 on the ephemeral tier.

Detection and alerting timeline (UTC):
- 2029-06-12 03:12 — Synthetic streaming checks p95 rising; alert threshold (streaming-p95>600ms) triggered.
- 2029-06-12 03:14 — On-call paged (SRE rotation); initial hypothesis: edge congestion.
- 2029-06-12 03:18 — Metrics show periodic cycles in prefetch-queue-depth and kv-prefetch-evictions tied to same cadence as latency spikes.
- 2029-06-12 03:30 — Scoped to clusters behind edge-proxy group A; autoscaler healthy, host CPU/GPU usage nominal.
- 2029-06-12 03:40 — Enabled emergency mitigation: reduce KV prefetch aggressiveness flag on edge-proxy (rollout to group A). Latency partial improvement.
- 2029-06-12 04:10 — Re-introduced jitter and backpressure at prefetch queue; observed stable p95 for ~20 minutes, then a different edge group started to show spikes.
- 2029-06-12 06:45 — Long-term mitigations started (see next actions). Incident declared resolved at 07:02 after changes propagated and alerts returned to baseline.

Initial hypothesis and root cause synthesis (short):
The sawtooth latency pattern resulted from correlated activity between two subsystems: the ephemeral session prefetcher and the edge multiplexing stack. The prefetcher runs heuristics to warm KV cache (prefix states and tokenizer metadata) for anticipated session continuation. Under certain traffic shapes the prefetcher batches aggressive reads, momentarily increasing KV cache pressure and triggering eviction cascades across the region. Edge multiplexers then experience transient increases in per-session fetch latency when the KV store returns misses/slow reads; because the multiplexer tries to amortize small I/O windows it briefly queues and coalesces streams, producing the observed periodic latency wave. The interaction is amplified by:
- Prefetch aggressiveness configured without jitter, causing synchronized waves across hosts.
- Eviction policy (LRU-ish) that compacts hot prefixes during a sustained memory pressure pulse, causing subsequent misses until the cache re-warms.
- Prefetch queue had no backpressure -> it amplified rather than smoothed bursts.

Evidence supporting hypothesis:
- Metric correlation: prefetch-queue-depth spikes temporally align with kv-prefetch-evictions and TTFB spikes.
- Flame graphs from host-side tracing show increased wait on kv-read RPCs during spike windows; CPU/GPU utilization flat, indicating I/O-driven delay.
- Canary experiment: toggling prefetch to conservative mode on a subset of hosts removed the sawtooth pattern for those hosts.

Why this mattered operationally:
- The pattern is noisy and short-lived; alerts for p95 alone are noisy and can lead to oscillatory mitigations.
- Without an operator-visible prefetch metric/alert, triage wasted time chasing edge config and autoscaler noise.

Immediate mitigations applied during the incident (what we did):
1) Scoped rollback of recent prefetch heuristic rollout (flag toggled) for group A (03:40 UTC) — reduced amplitude of waves for that group.
2) Applied exponential jitter to prefetch scheduling on a pilot subset (03:50 UTC).
3) Added short-term backpressure: limit concurrent prefetches to 6 per host and drop excess prefetches (04:05 UTC).
4) Temporarily increased KV store soft memory cap to avoid eviction cascade while we tune heuristics (04:20 UTC).
5) Rollout of backpressure + conservative prefetch to remaining edge groups (04:50–06:30 UTC) with staggered deployment windows to avoid synchronized behavior.

Operator commands & quick checks (for oncall):
- Check streaming TTFB and prefetch queue trends (Grafana): streaming.ttfb.p95, streaming.prefetch.queue_depth, kv.prefetch.evictions
- Live host trace (use flame traces): curl http://trace-host:9411/trace/active | grep kv:read
- Toggle prefetch feature flag (emergency): POST /admin/flags/prefetch_mode {"mode":"conservative"} (internal admin endpoint)
- Limit prefetch concurrency via sctl: sctl set edge.prefetch.max_concurrent=6 --cluster eu-west-1 --note "emergency backpressure"
- Validate KV slow RPCs: kubectl logs kv-frontend -n kv --since=15m | grep 'slow-rpc'

Runbook (draft) — detection, triage, mitigation
(Goal: allow oncall to quickly identify pattern and enact mitigations without broad rollouts)
1) Detection triggers
  - New composite alert: streaming-ttfb-sawtooth-pattern (requires p95 AND prefetch-queue-depth periodicity)
  - Secondary alert: kv-prefetch-evictions > 50/min for 5m
2) Triage checklist
  - Confirm geographic scope: which edge group(s) show synchronized spikes.
  - Check recent flag rollouts: prefetch heuristics, eviction-policy changes, edge-proxy binary versions.
  - Quick A/B test: flip one host pool to conservative prefetch mode. If that pool's p95 stabilizes, root cause likely prefetch-related.
3) Immediate mitigations (order matters)
  a) Apply conservative prefetch on smallest affected host subset first (min blast radius).
  b) Enable prefetch jitter (exponential backoff + random offset 0..Xs).
  c) Add/adjust prefetch backpressure: cap concurrent prefetches per host.
  d) If KV evictions remain high, temporarily raise soft memory cap for KV store until heuristics are tuned.
  e) Avoid broad autoscaler toggles; autoscaler changes can mask signals and increase noise.
4) Longer-term mitigations (post-incident)
  - Implement prefetch coordination algorithm to avoid cluster-wide synchronization (leaderless randomized staggering).
  - Make prefetch schedule and backpressure metrics emit at higher resolution (10s) and add them to default SLO dashboards.
  - Revisit KV eviction policy to detect and gracefully degrade prefetch throughput before evictions cascade.
  - Add canary gating for prefetch heuristics with automated rollback if evictions spike.

Monitoring & alert tuning recommendations
- New metrics to instrument: prefetch.jitter_applied (bool), prefetch.dropped_due_to_backpressure, kv.eviction_cascade_score (heuristic), prefetch.scheduled_batch_size.
- Composite alert (as above) to reduce noisy p95-only pages. Use a signal that requires both streaming p95 and prefetch/eviction indicators.
- Add a dashboard for streaming-plat-health that correlates prefetch and kv metrics with edge multiplexer queues and socket latency.

Follow-ups and ownership (concrete tickets and owners):
- SRE-482 (Linear) — Root-cause writeup and timeline (owner: Priya Rao) — due 2029-06-20.
- INFRA-1124 (GitHub) — Add prefetch backpressure controls + feature toggles (owner: Jun Park) — PR in review.
- SRE-507 — Add composite alert and dashboard panels (owner: Aisha Nadar) — due 2029-06-22.
- KV-239 — Evaluate eviction policy and soft cap autosizing (owner: Marcos Silva) — due 2029-07-05.

Post-incident notes (lessons learned):
- Feature rollouts that have cluster-wide effects must include randomized stagger windows by default. Synchronized heuristics are a systemic hazard.
- Observability gaps: prefetch and eviction metrics were too low-resolution and not on the default SRE dashboard.
- Triage playbooks need a short-memory A/B test pattern: flip a tiny pool first and use the result to confirm/deny hypotheses.

Open questions / next experiments:
- Can we move some prefetch work off hot-path I/O by using a local in-memory warming layer before hitting KV? (infra research ticket).
- Are there workload patterns (e.g., many short sessions with predictable next-token distributions) that make prefetch harmful? Need synthetic replay tests.

Appendix: quick troubleshooting checklist for oncall (one-page)
- Step 0: Check composite alert and narrow to edge groups.
- Step 1: Look at prefetch.queue_depth and kv.evictions graph at 10s resolution.
- Step 2: Flip a tiny host pool to conservative prefetch mode and watch p95 for 1–3 minutes.
- Step 3: If improvement, roll conservative mode + jitter + backpressure to other groups in staggered 5m windows.
- Step 4: If no improvement, escalate to infra/KV oncall and collect host flame traces.

Contact list for escalation:
- Priya Rao (SRE lead) — priya@redwood.ai
- Jun Park (edge infra) — jun@redwood.ai
- Marcos Silva (kv infra) — marcos@redwood.ai

Status: draft. This doc should be refined into two artifacts: (1) a compact operational runbook card for the oncall rotation, and (2) a formal postmortem with timeline and RCA once the tickets above land.

End of document.
